weeks.title: Place value to ten million

spell.rule: the Latin prefix ad- changes to match the next letter, giving a double consonant: ac-, at-, ap-, al- (accompany, attached, approach, allocate)

weeks.read: a longer novel of the child's choice from the library, to read through the half term

days.ma: Write digit cards 0–9 on paper scraps. Pick seven to make a number such as 4,072,815, read it aloud and say the value of every digit (the 4 is worth 4,000,000). Make and read four more.
days.en: Choose a library novel for this half term and start a Year 6 reading journal: the title, your first impressions after the opening chapter and two questions you hope the book will answer.

days.ma: Write 3,060,405 and 3,600,045 in words. Then write these in digits: seven million, eighty thousand and nine; two million, two hundred thousand, two hundred.
days.en: Grammar warm-up: on one page of your book find and label a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, determiner, pronoun and conjunction. Then underline the main clause in one long sentence.

days.ma: Order smallest to largest: 6,504,321; 6,540,321; 6,054,321; 650,432; 6,504,312. Write three comparisons using < and >, and explain which digit decided each one.
days.en: Handwriting speed test: copy a paragraph in joined writing for one minute and count the words. Try again aiming for the same neatness but more words, and decide when printed letters are better (labels, forms).

days.ma: Draw a 0 to 10,000,000 number line on a long strip of paper, marking each million. Mark 2,500,000 and 7,750,000 exactly, then estimate where 4,300,000 and 9,050,000 go and explain your thinking.
days.en: Word detective: 'accompany' is ad- + company and 'attached' is ad- + tach. Use a dictionary to find five words starting acc-, att-, app- or all- and write what each means.

days.ma: Quick check: the value of the 8 in 3,812,406; nine million and ninety in digits; 1,000,000 more than 8,450,000; the largest number using 3, 0, 7, 5, 1, 9, 2; a number between 4,999,000 and 5,000,000.
days.en: Quick check: summarise your book so far in five sentences, label the word classes in 'Several anxious passengers waited silently beside the old clock', and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Rounding and negative numbers

spell.rule: unstressed vowels you cannot hear clearly: say them in a 'spelling voice' (def-I-nite, sep-A-rate, fam-I-ly)

weeks.read: the half-term novel, paying close attention to the main character

days.ma: Round 4,587,362 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000. Set the answers out in a table and circle the rounding that changes the most digits.
days.en: Choose a moment in your novel when the main character's feelings change. Write what they feel, think and want, backing each point with a short quotation as evidence.

days.ma: Rounding puzzle: a number rounded to the nearest 100,000 is 3,200,000. What are the smallest and largest whole numbers it could be? Make up two puzzles like it for a parent.
days.en: Expanded noun phrases: turn 'the man' into 'the tall, nervous man in the dripping raincoat who never smiled'. Build three more for characters in your book.

days.ma: Draw a thermometer from −30 °C to 30 °C on paper. A mountain top is −14 °C and the valley is 9 °C: what is the difference? Make up four more temperature pairs that cross zero and find each difference.
days.en: Relative clauses: write five sentences about your book using who, which, whose, where and when, then one where the relative pronoun is left out ('The map [that] she found was torn').

days.ma: Real-life negatives: a bank balance of −£45 has £120 paid in; a diver at −80 m rises 35 m; a lift goes from floor −2 to floor 7. Find each new value, then count back in 7s from 30 to −33.
days.en: Plan and write a 150-word description of an invented character that shows their personality through actions and speech rather than telling ('She checked the lock three times' not 'She was worried').

days.ma: Quick check: round 7,449,999 to the nearest million and nearest 10,000; −12 + 19; the difference between −8 °C and 15 °C; order −4, −14, 4, 0, −1.
days.en: Quick check: read your character description aloud while the family guesses the personality trait; point out two relative clauses; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Mental and written adding and subtracting

spell.rule: the /sh/ sound spelt sc or ci before a vowel (conscious, conscience, delicious, precious); learn the difference in meaning between the two words

weeks.read: a story with a richly described setting, such as a ghost story or fantasy adventure

days.ma: Mental methods, said aloud: 4,600,000 + 2,700,000; 4,567 + 999 (add 1,000, take away 1); 8,000,000 − 3,250,000; 72,000 − 39,500. Explain each method to a parent.
days.en: Find a setting description in your book. Highlight similes, metaphors and personification and explain what each one makes the reader feel.

days.ma: Column methods: 3,456,789 + 1,987,654 and 6,000,000 − 2,345,678. Check each with the inverse operation.
days.en: Thesaurus work: find four synonyms each for 'dark', 'cold' and 'quiet'. Rank each set from weakest to strongest and choose the best for a spooky forest.

days.ma: Estimate first, then calculate: 48,912 + 21,377 − 9,845. Was your estimate close? Decide whether rounding to the nearest 1,000 or 10,000 gave a more useful check.
days.en: Commas for clarity: compare 'Let's eat, Grandma!' with 'Let's eat Grandma!' Write four sentences where moving or adding a comma changes the meaning.

days.ma: A stadium holds 72,500. On Saturday 68,349 people came; on Sunday 4,812 fewer came. How many seats were empty on Sunday? Write down which operations you chose and why, then invent a problem of your own.
days.en: Write a two-paragraph description of an abandoned place, such as an empty fairground, using three senses, figurative language and a mix of short and long sentences to build atmosphere.

days.ma: Quick check: 2,500,000 + 750,000; 405,026 − 198,754; estimate 6,912 + 3,105 to the nearest thousand; a two-step word problem a parent makes up.
days.en: Quick check: read your setting aloud and ask the family which image worked best; add commas to three tricky sentences; spell 'conscious' and 'conscience' in sentences that show the difference.

weeks.title: Factors, multiples and primes

spell.rule: silent or easily missed letters: say every sound slowly (twelfth, February, Wednesday, environment)

weeks.read: a story with lots of dialogue, noticing how speech shows what characters are like

days.ma: Find all the factor pairs of 36, 48 and 60 by drawing arrays of dots. Which number has the most factors?
days.en: Find three examples of parenthesis in your reading (brackets, dashes or commas). Discuss why the author added the extra information and whether the sentence works without it.

days.ma: Common factors: list the factors of 24 and 36 in a Venn diagram. What is the highest common factor? Repeat for 45 and 60.
days.en: Rewrite five plain sentences adding parenthesis, using each type at least once, e.g. 'The old lighthouse – empty for years – stood on the cliff.'

days.ma: Common multiples: two buses leave together at 09:00, one every 6 minutes and one every 8 minutes. When do they next leave together? Find the lowest common multiple of 4, 6 and 10.
days.en: Write an eight-line argument between two characters over a treasure map. Start a new line for each speaker, punctuate speech correctly and add actions between lines.

days.ma: Draw a 1–100 grid and cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (but not the numbers themselves) to find every prime up to 100. Then draw a factor tree for 60.
days.en: Swap your dialogue with a parent to check the punctuation. Change 'said' where a better verb or an action helps, then read it aloud in character.

days.ma: Quick check: is 91 prime? the highest common factor of 18 and 30; the lowest common multiple of 9 and 12; three primes between 40 and 60; the first five square numbers and the first three cube numbers.
days.en: Quick check: punctuate a short dialogue a parent writes without any punctuation, add parenthesis to two sentences, and spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Long multiplication

spell.rule: words ending -cient and -tient, where the ending sounds like 'shunt' (sufficient, ancient, efficient, patient)

weeks.read: a mystery or detective story, stopping before the reveal to predict

days.ma: Warm up: 34 × 20 and 34 × 3, then put them together to find 34 × 23. Draw it as a grid so you can see why long multiplication works.
days.en: Read your mystery up to a cliffhanger. Predict who is responsible and what happens next, using one clue that is stated and one that is only hinted at.

days.ma: Long multiplication: estimate first, then calculate 243 × 36 and 1,524 × 27. Compare each answer with its estimate.
days.en: Modal verbs and adverbs: write sentences about who the culprit might be, moving from 'possibly' to 'definitely' (might, could, should, will, must, perhaps, surely).

days.ma: Long multiplication: 3,456 × 48 and 2,709 × 63. Take extra care with the zero placeholder in the second row.
days.en: Plan your own mystery: a detective, a crime, three suspects, two real clues and one false clue. Decide who the audience is and what tone you want.

days.ma: Problems: a farmer plants 38 rows of 425 trees; 245 pairs of shoes cost £37 each. Then spot the mistake: someone wrote 467 × 32 = 2,335. What went wrong and what is the right answer?
days.en: Write the opening scene where the crime is discovered. Use modal verbs in the detective's thoughts to show what they are unsure about.

days.ma: Quick check: 507 × 24; 1,836 × 45; estimate 3,980 × 21; explain to a parent why the second row of a long multiplication ends with a zero.
days.en: Quick check: was your prediction right? Order these from least to most certain: might, will, could, must, perhaps. Spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Short and long division

spell.rule: -ent words become -ence or -ency nouns (convenient → convenience, frequent → frequency, decent → decency)

weeks.read: more mystery stories, looking at how authors hide clues

days.ma: Short division: 5,736 ÷ 8 and 4,932 ÷ 12. Write the 12 times table down the side first if it helps.
days.en: The perfect form: write five sentences that show one thing happened before another, e.g. 'By the time the inspector arrived, the thief had escaped.' Underline each 'had' + verb.

days.ma: Long division: list the first ten multiples of 24, then calculate 7,248 ÷ 24. Do the same for 4,356 ÷ 18.
days.en: Write the middle of your mystery: the detective gathers clues. Include a short flashback using the past perfect.

days.ma: 3,659 ÷ 15 by long division. Write the answer three ways: with a remainder, as a mixed number and rounded to the nearest whole number.
days.en: Write the ending with the reveal, making sure every clue is explained.

days.ma: Remainders in context: 1,000 pupils travel in coaches of 52 seats – how many coaches? 750 eggs go into boxes of 12 – how many full boxes? £1,000 is shared by 16 people – how much each? Explain why each answer is rounded differently.
days.en: Edit and proof-read your whole mystery: check tenses stay consistent, verbs agree with their subjects, and look up any doubtful spelling in a dictionary.

days.ma: Quick check: 6,174 ÷ 7; 5,940 ÷ 36; 2,000 ÷ 24 as a remainder and as a mixed number; one context question a parent writes where you must decide whether to round up or down.
days.en: Quick check: perform your mystery to the family with expression and pace; they listen for the past perfect. Spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Consolidation: place value and the four operations

spell.rule: review: unstressed vowels, double consonants and -cient/-ence endings

weeks.read: finish the half-term novel and write a short recommendation

days.ma: Build a seven-digit number from digit cards; read it, write it in words and round it to the nearest 10,000 and 1,000,000. Repeat three times.
days.en: Choose your best piece from this half term (character description, setting or mystery). Re-read it and improve three word choices using a thesaurus.

days.ma: Find the difference between −15 °C and 22 °C; list the factors of 72; find every prime between 70 and 90.
days.en: Proof-read a paragraph a parent writes with ten deliberate mistakes (spellings, capitals, commas, speech marks, tense). Can you find them all?

days.ma: 2,307 × 46 by long multiplication and 8,544 ÷ 32 by long division. Check each answer by estimating.
days.en: Dictionary race: a parent calls out eight words; use the first three or four letters to find each quickly and write its meaning in your own words.

days.ma: A charity needs £12,000. 28 people each raise £385. How much more is needed? Use rounding to check your answer is sensible.
days.en: Book talk: discuss your novel with a parent for 10 minutes. Build on each other's points or disagree politely, giving a reason every time.

days.ma: Half-term check: write 5,030,300 in words; round 6,849,500 to the nearest 100,000; −9 + 17; 3,000,000 − 1,456,789; 625 × 34; 4,416 ÷ 16; the highest common factor of 28 and 42. Mark together and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: write a five-sentence recommendation of your novel with reasons, and take a test on the half term's spelling words.

weeks.title: Order of operations and multi-step problems

spell.rule: silent h after another consonant (vehicle, ghost, rhyme, rhubarb, exhaust)

weeks.read: a non-fiction book or report about inventions and discoveries

days.ma: Calculate 3 + 4 × 5 two ways and discuss which is right. Learn the order: brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −. Try 20 − 12 ÷ 4, (20 − 12) ÷ 4 and 6 × (7 + 3) − 15.
days.en: Read about an invention. Retrieve six facts and record them in a table: what it is, when it appeared, how it works and why it mattered.

days.ma: Add brackets to make each one true: 8 + 4 × 3 = 36; 30 − 6 ÷ 3 = 8; 5 × 6 − 2 + 1 = 21. Then make up two of your own.
days.en: Active and passive: 'The engineer tested the rocket' becomes 'The rocket was tested by the engineer.' Change six active sentences into the passive and label the subject in each.

days.ma: Four fours: make every number from 1 to 10 using exactly four 4s and any operations and brackets, e.g. (4 + 4) ÷ (4 + 4) = 1.
days.en: Why use the passive? Find three passive sentences in a non-fiction text or news article and explain why the writer hid or delayed the doer (unknown, unimportant or obvious).

days.ma: Bake sale: 48 cakes sell at 75p and 36 biscuits at 40p. Ingredients cost £18.50. What is the profit? Write it as one calculation with brackets, then estimate to check.
days.en: Write a short report of a kitchen experiment (e.g. dissolving sugar in warm and cold water) almost entirely in the passive: 'The water was measured…'

days.ma: Quick check: 7 + 3 × 8; (7 + 3) × 8; 100 − 36 ÷ 4 × 2; add brackets so 12 − 4 × 2 = 16; a two-step money problem from a parent.
days.en: Quick check: turn three active sentences into the passive and two passive into the active; explain 'subject' and 'object' using an example; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Simplifying and comparing fractions

spell.rule: prefix sub- changes to match the next letter (suggest, support, suppose, succeed, suffix)

weeks.read: a discussion text or newspaper debate page that gives two sides of an issue

days.ma: Fold paper strips into halves, quarters and eighths, and others into thirds, sixths and twelfths. Use them to write three equivalents each for 2/3 and 3/4.
days.en: Read a discussion text. List the arguments for and against, then mark each one as fact or opinion and explain how you can tell.

days.ma: Simplify using the highest common factor: 12/18, 24/36, 15/45, 42/56. Say which factor you divided by each time.
days.en: Semi-colons join two closely related main clauses: 'Some people love homework; others think it wastes time.' Write six for-and-against pairs like this about whether ten-year-olds should have their own phones.

days.ma: Compare by making common denominators: 3/4 or 5/7? 5/6 or 7/9? 2/3 or 7/11? Use a common multiple each time.
days.en: Semi-colons in lists of longer items: 'We visited Leeds, a city in Yorkshire; Cardiff, the capital of Wales; and Belfast.' Write two lists like this of your own.

days.ma: Order 7/4, 1 1/2, 5/3 and 11/8 by changing them all to twenty-fourths. Mark them on a number line from 0 to 2.
days.en: Plan a balanced argument: 'Should school uniform be scrapped?' Note the audience, purpose, introduction, points for, points against and a conclusion with your view.

days.ma: Quick check: simplify 18/24 and 35/50; which is greater, 4/9 or 5/12? order 9/5, 1 3/4 and 17/10; give two fractions equivalent to 3/5.
days.en: Quick check: give your opinion on uniform with two reasons; correct three sentences where a semi-colon is used wrongly; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Adding and subtracting fractions

spell.rule: double letters that are easy to miss: say them separately (exaggerate, embarrass, accommodate, necessary)

weeks.read: persuasive letters, adverts and opinion columns found around the house or online

days.ma: Draw rectangles to show 1/3 + 1/4, 2/5 + 3/10 and 5/6 − 1/4, finding a common denominator for each.
days.en: Write the introduction and the arguments for in your balanced argument on school uniform.

days.ma: Answers greater than 1: 3/4 + 5/6 and 7/8 + 2/3. Write each answer as an improper fraction and as a mixed number.
days.en: Colons: use one to introduce a list ('You will need three things: …') and one to explain ('The verdict was clear: uniform stays.'). Then use a dash between two clauses for a chattier effect. Write three of each.

days.ma: Mixed numbers: 2 1/3 + 1 3/4 and 4 1/5 − 1 1/2. Try both methods: whole numbers first, or turning into improper fractions.
days.en: Finish the balanced argument (arguments against and a conclusion), using at least one semi-colon, one colon and one dash correctly.

days.ma: A recipe uses 1 3/4 cups of flour for bread and 2/3 of a cup for biscuits. The bag holds 4 cups. How much is left? Draw a bar model to show it.
days.en: Family mini-debate on your topic: each speaker has one minute using notes, then one minute to answer the other side politely.
Quick check: explain the difference between a colon and a semi-colon with an example of each; punctuate four sentences a parent gives you; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions

spell.rule: adding suffixes to words ending in a single consonant: double it when the last syllable is stressed and the suffix starts with a vowel (equip → equipped, but equipment)

weeks.read: a children's newspaper or news website, reading one report a day

days.ma: Draw a square and shade 1/2. Shade 1/3 of that half in another colour to show 1/3 × 1/2 = 1/6. Draw 1/4 × 1/2 and 2/3 × 3/4 the same way.
days.en: Read a news report. Label the headline, the opening paragraph that answers who, what, where, when and why, a quotation and the ending. Retrieve five facts.

days.ma: Multiply and simplify: 3/5 × 2/3; 3/4 × 5/6; 4/7 × 1/2. Can you spot a shortcut by simplifying before you multiply?
days.en: Hyphens to avoid ambiguity: compare 'a man-eating shark' with 'a man eating shark', and 're-cover' with 'recover'. Write five sentences with hyphenated adjectives such as 'a well-known singer' or 'a five-year-old boy'.

days.ma: Divide by a whole number: draw half a pizza and share it between 3 to show 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6. Then 3/4 ÷ 3, 2/5 ÷ 4 and 4/9 ÷ 2.
days.en: Words often confused: affect/effect, practice/practise, licence/license, stationary/stationery, passed/past. Write a sentence for each that shows the difference.

days.ma: 2/3 of a garden is grass and 3/4 of the grass has been mown. What fraction of the whole garden is mown? A 3/4 litre jug is shared between 6 cups: how much in each?
days.en: Write a news report about a made-up local event (such as a runaway goat at the school fair) with a headline, a strong opening, a quotation, a passive sentence and a hyphenated adjective.

days.ma: Quick check: 1/4 × 1/3; 5/6 × 3/5; 3/5 ÷ 3; 5/8 ÷ 2; a word problem a parent makes up about sharing part of a cake.
days.en: Quick check: read your report aloud like a newsreader; add hyphens to 'a little used path' and 'twenty one year old cars' so they make sense; spell 'equipped' and 'equipment'.

weeks.title: Converting units of measure

spell.rule: verbs ending in a consonant + y change y to i before -ed and -es, but keep y before -ing (occupy → occupied, occupies, occupying)

weeks.read: explanation texts and information leaflets with headings, bullet points and diagrams

days.ma: Weigh three kitchen items in grams and write each in kilograms (375 g = 0.375 kg). Then convert 2.45 kg and 0.06 kg to grams.
days.en: Study an information leaflet or explanation. How do the headings, subheadings, bullet points, bold words and diagrams help the reader find and understand information?

days.ma: Measure a room in centimetres and write it in metres and millimetres. Convert 3.405 km to metres and 72 mm to centimetres and metres.
days.en: Bullet points: either every point starts with a lower-case letter with no full stop, or every point is a full sentence. Rewrite a messy bulleted list so it is consistent, introduced by a colon.

days.ma: Miles and kilometres: 5 miles is about 8 km. Draw a conversion graph on squared paper from 0 to 50 miles and use it to convert 20 miles, 40 km and 30 miles. Then work out 100 miles without the graph.
days.en: Cohesion: highlight the words that link paragraphs in an explanation (as a result, meanwhile, this means, pronouns and synonyms). Rewrite a short paragraph with better links.

days.ma: Time and capacity: 3.5 hours in minutes; 150 seconds in minutes; minutes in a day. How many 250 ml glasses can be filled from a 1.5 litre bottle?
days.en: Write an explanation leaflet, such as how to care for a houseplant or how the moon seems to change shape, with a title, subheadings, consistent bullet points and a labelled diagram.

days.ma: Quick check: 4.2 km in m; 650 g in kg; 2.03 l in ml; 25 miles in km; a recipe needs 1.2 kg of potatoes and you have 850 g – how much more?
days.en: Quick check: check your leaflet against a list of features; use a dictionary to check three technical words; spell this week's word and its -ed and -ing forms.

weeks.title: Coordinates in four quadrants

spell.rule: two Latin prefixes with double letters: re- + commend and cor- (from con-) + respond

weeks.read: a collection of classic and modern poems; choose one to learn by heart

days.ma: Draw x and y axes from −6 to 6 on squared paper. Plot (3, 4), (−2, 5), (−4, −1) and (5, −3) and name the quadrant each point is in.
days.en: Read several poems from a collection. Choose one to learn by heart and talk about its theme and shape on the page.

days.ma: Play a hidden-shapes game with a parent on a four-quadrant grid: each hides a square and a triangle and you take turns calling coordinates until all are found.
days.en: Imagery hunt: find a metaphor, personification, alliteration and onomatopoeia in poems and explain the effect each has on the reader.

days.ma: Draw a triangle at (1, 2), (4, 2) and (1, 5). Translate it 5 left and 3 down and write the new coordinates. What do you notice about the numbers?
days.en: Silent letters: sort knight, psalm, solemn, doubt, island, wrestle, gnome and scissors by their silent letter, and make up a memory trick for the two hardest.

days.ma: Reflect the same triangle in the y-axis, then in the x-axis. Use a mirror or fold the paper to check, and record both sets of coordinates.
days.en: Write your own winter poem built around one extended metaphor (e.g. frost as a thief). Rehearse reading it aloud.

days.ma: Quick check: find the fourth corner of a square at (−2, 1), (2, 1) and (2, 5); reflect (3, −4) in the x-axis; translate (−5, 2) 6 right and 4 down.
days.en: Quick check: perform your learned poem by heart, using tone, volume and pauses to bring out the meaning; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Consolidation: calculation, fractions, measures and coordinates

spell.rule: review: lightning (a flash in a storm) and lightening (making lighter), plus this half term's homophones

weeks.read: a winter poem or seasonal story, read aloud as a family

days.ma: Calculate 50 − 6 × 7 and (50 − 6) × 7; simplify 32/48; order 5/8, 2/3 and 7/12.
days.en: Choose your best writing from this half term (balanced argument, news report or leaflet) and improve it using a checklist of that text type's features.
Grammar hunt in your own writing: find a passive sentence, a semi-colon, a colon, a hyphen, a relative clause and a modal verb. Add any that are missing.

days.ma: Winter biscuit recipe: 250 g butter, 0.4 kg flour, 125 g sugar. Write each in kg, find the total mass, and work out the amounts for half a batch.
days.en: Proof-read a paragraph a parent writes with ten punctuation and spelling mistakes, including homophones.

days.ma: Plot a star or snowflake shape in all four quadrants, then reflect it in one axis and write all the new coordinates.
days.en: Grammar terms quiz: a parent says a sentence and you name the features: subject, object, passive, relative clause, modal verb, parenthesis, colon.

days.ma: Half-term check: 18 + 12 ÷ 3; simplify 27/36; 1 3/5 + 2/3; 3/4 × 2/9; 3.5 km in m; 15 miles in km; reflect (−4, 2) in the y-axis. Mark together and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: read a winter story or poem aloud with expression, then take the half-term spelling test.

weeks.title: Ratio and proportion

spell.rule: formal words with letters you do not hear: parliament (the 'ia' is hardly said), government, February

weeks.read: formal letters, official notices and the opening of a formal speech

days.ma: Use dried pasta and beans: lay out 2 beans for every 3 pasta pieces and write 2:3. Build 4:6 and 10:15 and explain why they are the same ratio.
days.en: Compare an informal message and a formal letter about the same news. List the differences: contractions, word choices ('ask' or 'request'), the passive and how the writer addresses the reader.

days.ma: Pancakes for 4 need 100 g flour, 2 eggs and 300 ml milk. Write the amounts for 6 people and for 10 people. If you can, make a half batch together.
days.en: Formal swaps: get → obtain, find out → discover, help → assist, ask for → request. Rewrite six chatty sentences so they suit a formal letter.

days.ma: Unequal sharing: share 35 sweets in the ratio 2:5 using a bar model. Then share £60 in the ratio 1:3 and 84 stickers in the ratio 3:4.
days.en: The subjunctive in formal writing: 'If I were in charge…', 'I insist that he be on time', 'It is vital that every pupil arrive early.' Write five sentences of your own.

days.ma: A class has boys and girls in the ratio 3:4 and 28 children altogether. How many girls are there? What fraction of the class are boys? Make up a similar problem about your family.
days.en: Write a formal letter to the local council asking for a new bench or crossing near the park. Use formal vocabulary, the passive once and at least one subjunctive.

days.ma: Quick check: simplify 12:18; paint is mixed 3 parts blue to 1 part white – how much blue goes with 2 litres of white? share 72 in the ratio 5:3; a recipe for 4 uses 150 g of rice – how much for 10?
days.en: Quick check: read your letter aloud as if at a council meeting; turn three informal sentences into formal ones; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Scale factors and similar shapes

spell.rule: words ending -ege with no d, unlike -edge (privilege, college, sacrilege – but knowledge, hedge)

weeks.read: a biography of an inspiring person from history (non-fiction)

days.ma: Draw a 3 cm × 2 cm rectangle. Enlarge it by scale factor 2 and scale factor 3. Measure the new sides and perimeters: what do you notice?
days.en: Read a chapter of a biography and make a timeline of the key events, with a date or age for each.

days.ma: A triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm is enlarged so the shortest side is 12 cm. What is the scale factor and what are the other sides? Make up two similar puzzles.
days.en: Summarise three paragraphs of the biography in one sentence each, then pick out the key detail that supports each main idea.

days.ma: Make a scale plan of your bedroom on squared paper where 1 cm represents 50 cm. Measure the room and the main furniture first.
days.en: Interview a grandparent or family friend about their childhood, school and first job. Take notes as they talk, using abbreviations and keywords.

days.ma: Map scales: on a map 1 cm represents 2 km. How far is a route of 7.5 cm? How long on the map is a 13 km walk? Measure a route on a real map at home if you have one.
days.en: Write a short biography of the person you interviewed in the third person and past tense, with a paragraph for each stage of life.

days.ma: Quick check: the scale factor from a 5 cm side to a 20 cm side; a 6 cm × 4 cm photo enlarged so its width is 15 cm – how tall?; a 3.5 cm line on a 1 cm : 50 cm plan in real life.
days.en: Quick check: a dictionary race using the first three or four letters of eight words; read your biography to the person it is about; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Algebra: formulae and sequences

spell.rule: -ous adjectives drop the u when -ity is added (curious → curiosity, generous → generosity)

weeks.read: an extract from a classic novel written over a hundred years ago (many are free online)

days.ma: Make a row of squares from matchsticks or cotton buds: 1 square uses 4, 2 squares use 7, 3 squares use 10. Find the rule and predict how many for 20 squares. Check by building a few more.
days.en: Read a classic extract aloud. List six unfamiliar or old-fashioned words, guess their meaning from the sentence, then check in a dictionary.

days.ma: Find the rule and the 10th term: 5, 9, 13, 17…; 2, 8, 14, 20…; 30, 27, 24, 21… Describe each rule in words and as a formula using n.
days.en: Root words: use 'bene' (good), 'mal' (bad), 'cred' (believe) and 'circum' (around) to work out benevolent, malicious, incredulous and circumference, then find one more word for each root.

days.ma: A taxi costs £3 plus £2 per mile, so C = 3 + 2m. Find the cost of 8 miles and of 15 miles. Use P = 2(l + w) to find the perimeter of a 7 cm × 4.5 cm rectangle.
days.en: Compare a paragraph of the classic with a paragraph of a modern novel: sentence length, vocabulary and how speech is punctuated. What has changed?

days.ma: A roast takes 40 minutes per kilogram plus 20 minutes: t = 40k + 20. Find t for 1.5 kg and 4.5 kg. Write your own formula for saving pocket money each week.
days.en: Inference: explain what a character in the classic wants and why, using point, evidence and explanation in one paragraph.

days.ma: Quick check: the next two terms and the rule for 7, 12, 17, 22; if a = 4 and b = 3, find 5a − 2b; use C = 3 + 2m to find the miles for a £21 journey.
days.en: Quick check: retell the extract in modern language in five sentences; explain three new words using their roots; spell 'curious' and 'curiosity'.

weeks.title: Algebra: equations and unknowns

spell.rule: -ity nouns formed from adjectives and Latin roots (community, identity, ability, electricity)

weeks.read: a traditional tale or modern story from another culture

days.ma: Missing numbers as algebra: 3 × □ + 5 = 26 becomes 3n + 5 = 26. Model it with cups hiding counters on one side of a 'balance' and coins on the other, then solve it.
days.en: Read a tale from another culture. Identify its theme (such as greed or kindness) and its conventions (a wise elder, a test repeated three times, a lesson at the end).

days.ma: Solve: 4x − 7 = 29; 2y + 15 = 51; 60 ÷ a = 12; a + a + 9 = 35. Check each by substituting your answer back in.
days.en: Compare it with a traditional tale you know well. Make a table of similarities and differences in characters, setting and lesson.

days.ma: Two unknowns: list every whole-number pair where a + b = 12. Which pair also makes a − b = 4? Then find all whole-number pairs for 3c + d = 20.
days.en: Plan your own tale in the same style, with a clear lesson. Decide who it is for and borrow two conventions from the tale you read.

days.ma: Combinations: with 3 tops and 4 pairs of trousers, how many outfits? Use a table or tree so you do not miss any. How many two-digit codes can be made from the digits 1–4?
days.en: Write your tale, including dialogue that moves the action on and a final line that delivers the lesson.

days.ma: Quick check: 5n − 4 = 31; two pairs of whole numbers for 2x + y = 10; how many meals can be made from 3 starters and 4 main courses?; write 'a number doubled, then add 7, is 25' as an equation and solve it.
days.en: Quick check: hold a family discussion on whether your tale's lesson still matters today; challenge views politely with reasons; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Decimals to three places

spell.rule: -ive adjectives and double letters from the Latin prefix ad- (aggressive, attractive, appreciative)

weeks.read: an information book about an animal or habitat

days.ma: Draw a place value grid from thousands to thousandths. Write 4.073 and say the value of each digit. Order 0.405, 0.45, 0.054 and 0.5.
days.en: Read three paragraphs of an information book. Underline the key points and cross out examples and extra details.
Précis: shrink a 150-word passage to 50 words without losing its meaning. Count the words and keep cutting.

days.ma: Multiply decimals by whole numbers: 3.45 × 6; 0.79 × 8; 4.08 × 7. Then: 7 notebooks cost £1.35 each – what is the total?
days.en: Precise words: replace wordy phrases ('a large number of' → 'many', 'at this moment in time' → 'now'). Find synonyms and antonyms for five words using a thesaurus.

days.ma: Division with decimal answers: 47 ÷ 4; 98 ÷ 8; £15 shared between 4; 63 ÷ 5. Keep dividing by adding zeros after the decimal point.
days.en: Make a fact file about your animal from your notes, then write a 30-word summary of the whole thing.

days.ma: Quick check: the value of the 9 in 2.019; 0.35 × 1,000; 6.4 ÷ 100; 2.75 × 9; 87 ÷ 4 to two decimal places.
days.en: Quick check: précis a paragraph a parent chooses into one sentence; explain 'synonym', 'antonym' and 'ellipsis' with examples; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Consolidation: ratio, algebra and decimals

spell.rule: review: -ise verbs built from nouns (critic → criticise, apology → apologise, memory → memorise)

weeks.read: a non-fiction book on a topic of the child's choice, for a short presentation

days.ma: Share 90 in the ratio 4:5; a model car is 1:20 of a 3.6 m real car – how long is the model?; find the 15th term of 4, 10, 16, 22…
days.en: Pick your best writing of this half term (formal letter, biography or tale). Highlight one strength and one thing to improve, then edit it.

days.ma: Solve 6n + 11 = 47; find all whole-number pairs for x + 2y = 10; write a formula for the cost of tickets at £4.50 each plus a £2 booking fee.
days.en: Handwriting for presentation: write the title page of your talk in your neatest joined writing and choose the best pen for headings and for notes.

days.ma: Decimals: 0.067 × 100; 5.3 ÷ 1,000; 6.48 × 7; 74 ÷ 8 to two decimal places.
days.en: Prepare a two-minute talk about your non-fiction topic, using notes on a small card rather than a script.

days.ma: Recipe problem: a smoothie uses banana and yoghurt in the ratio 2:3. With 450 g of yoghurt, how much banana? If bananas weigh 0.125 kg each, how many are needed?
days.en: Give your talk to the family, then answer two questions using your notes and the correct technical words.

days.ma: Half-term check: share 56 in the ratio 3:5; a 4 cm side enlarged by scale factor 2.5; the 20th term of 3, 7, 11…; 3y − 8 = 22; 3 outfits from 2 hats and 3 scarves?; 4.06 × 6; 9 ÷ 4. Mark together and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: name the grammar feature in four sentences a parent reads out, then take the half-term spelling test.

weeks.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages + arithmetic revision

spell.rule: ph for the /f/ sound in words from Greek (physical, photograph, sphere, phrase)

weeks.read: short SATs-style texts: a story extract, a non-fiction article and a poem (sample papers are free online)

days.ma: Fractions are divisions: draw 3 pizzas shared between 4 people to show 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4. Then use short division (3.000 ÷ 8) to turn 3/8, 5/8 and 1/3 into decimals.
days.en: Retrieval: read a short non-fiction article and answer five 'find and copy' questions in under 10 minutes. Underline where each answer came from.

days.ma: Make matching cards for 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 1/10, 1/20, 1/8 and 1/3 as fractions, decimals and percentages. Play pairs face down.
days.en: Word meaning: answer questions like 'Find and copy one word that means…' and 'Which word shows the character was nervous?' using context and root words.

days.ma: Percentages of amounts using 10%, 5% and 1%: 15% of 360; 35% of £80; 12% of 250 g; 95% of 60. Explain your building blocks.
days.en: Read a story extract. Complete a true/false table about it and put five events in order, numbering them 1 to 5.

days.ma: Comparing with percentages: 18/25 in one quiz and 34/40 in another – which is the better score? A £60 coat with 15% off or with £10 off? Find 2/3 of £50 to the nearest penny.
days.en: Grammar in SATs style: say whether 'round' is a noun, verb, adjective or preposition in four different sentences, then do the same with 'light' and 'before'.

days.ma: Quick check (SATs style): 7/8 as a decimal; 30% of 450; order 0.6, 5/8 and 62%; 1/3 of 100 to two decimal places; 4,826 + 1,375 − 999 mentally.
days.en: Quick check: a 15-minute mini reading paper a parent sets from a short text (four retrieval and two vocabulary questions); spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Area and perimeter + arithmetic revision

spell.rule: British spellings that differ from American ones (programme, colour, centre, travelled)

weeks.read: a story extract with a tense or emotional moment

days.ma: Arithmetic warm-up: 2,345 × 26 and 3,672 ÷ 17. Then cut 24 squares from scrap paper and arrange them into every possible rectangle with area 24 cm², recording each perimeter.
days.en: Inference: how does a character feel at a key moment? Give two pieces of evidence from the text and explain what each shows.

days.ma: Make a loop of string 30 cm long and form rectangles with a perimeter of 30 cm on squared paper. Which one has the largest area? Are any squares possible?
days.en: Practise three-mark answers: make a point, quote evidence and explain it. Write two answers about the same character's motives.

days.ma: Cut a rectangle along its diagonal to show a triangle is half of a rectangle. Use area = ½ × base × height for triangles with base 8 cm, height 5 cm; base 12 cm, height 7 cm; base 9 cm, height 6 cm.
days.en: Passive revision: rewrite five active sentences from the story in the passive and explain how it changes the focus of each sentence.

days.ma: Cut a triangle off one end of a paper parallelogram and slide it to the other end to make a rectangle. Use area = base × height for 9 cm × 4 cm and 7.5 cm × 6 cm. When can you not use a formula?
days.en: Edit a paragraph a parent writes that keeps switching tense and has verbs that do not agree with their subjects.

days.ma: Quick check: area of a triangle with base 14 cm and height 6 cm; a parallelogram with base 11 cm and height 5 cm; two rectangles with area 36 cm² but different perimeters; area of an L-shape a parent draws.
days.en: Quick check: a 15-minute mini reading paper with two inference questions and one three-mark explanation; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Volume + reasoning revision

spell.rule: -ssion after a root ending in ss or mit (profess → profession, admit → admission, discuss → discussion)

weeks.read: a longer non-fiction article, for example about an expedition or a scientific discovery

days.ma: Using sugar cubes, dice or same-sized building bricks, build cuboids that each use exactly 24 cubes. Record the length, width and height of each.
days.en: Summary: give each paragraph of an article a short title, then choose which sentence best sums up the whole article and say why.

days.ma: Measure an empty food box, a shoebox and a tissue box. Estimate, then calculate, each volume in cm³ using length × width × height.
days.en: Punctuation revision: write a sentence each using a semi-colon, a colon before a list, a colon before an explanation and a dash between two clauses.

days.ma: Volume problems: a cube with 7 cm edges; a 12 × 5 × 4 cm cuboid; a cuboid with volume 360 cm³, length 9 cm and width 5 cm – what is the height?
days.en: More punctuation: hyphens, brackets, inverted commas and apostrophes for plural possession (the girls' coats, the children's books). Correct six sentences a parent writes.

days.ma: Bigger and smaller units: estimate the volume of your room in m³. How many cm³ in 1 m³? A tank is 50 cm × 30 cm × 20 cm – how many litres does it hold (1,000 cm³ = 1 litre)?
days.en: Proof-read a page of your own writing from this year, checking only punctuation, then only spelling.

days.ma: Quick check: volume of a 5 cm cube; a 2.5 m × 2 m × 3 m skip; how many 2 cm cubes fit in a 10 × 10 × 6 cm box?; 3,600 ml in litres; a two-step problem a parent sets.
days.en: Quick check: a 15-minute mini reading paper with a summary and a sequencing question; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Statistics: line graphs, pie charts and the mean

spell.rule: the prefix contra- or contro- means 'against' (controversy, contradict, contrary)

weeks.read: poems on one theme, such as the sea, and a descriptive story extract

days.ma: Measure the hand spans of five family members in cm and find the mean. Then find the mean of 12, 15, 9, 18 and 21.
days.en: Language questions: 'What does the phrase … suggest about …?' Pick three phrases from a poem and explain what each suggests and the effect on the reader.

days.ma: Working backwards: four numbers have a mean of 9 and three of them are 7, 10 and 12. What is the fourth? Record the daily maximum temperature from a weather forecast for a week and find the mean.
days.en: Look at a poem's structure: verses, line lengths, rhyme and rhythm. How does the shape of the poem help create its mood?

days.ma: Push a stick upright into the ground or a pot and measure its shadow every hour today (two minutes each time). Draw a line graph of the results and describe the pattern.
days.en: Compare two poems on the same theme: which uses language more powerfully? Give two reasons with quotations.

days.ma: Pie charts: 24 people chose fruit – 6 apple, 8 banana, 4 orange, 6 grapes. Work out each fraction of 360° and draw the pie chart round a plate. In another chart of 60 children, 90° is football: how many children is that?
days.en: Choose a short poem to learn by heart and rehearse it, deciding where to pause, slow down or change volume.

days.ma: Quick check: the mean of 4.5, 6 and 7.5; in a pie chart of 120 people, 1/3 walk – how many and what angle?; read two values from your shadow graph; 25% of 360°.
days.en: Quick check: perform your poem from memory, then answer a 15-minute mini paper on a poem; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Angles and properties of shapes

spell.rule: verbs ending -ine sound like 'in' and drop the e before -ed (determine → determined, examine → examined, imagine → imagined)

weeks.read: a persuasive leaflet and a factual report on the same topic

days.ma: Draw two crossing straight lines and measure the four angles. Which are equal? Find missing angles: 180° − 57° on a line, and 110°, 95°, 80° and ? around a point.
days.en: Fact or opinion: sort ten statements from a persuasive leaflet and a factual report, explaining the clue words ('best', 'should', 'research shows').

days.ma: Draw a triangle, tear off its three corners and line them up to show they make 180°. Find missing angles: 48° and 67°; an isosceles triangle with a top angle of 40°.
days.en: Prediction questions: given the opening of a story extract, predict what will happen and back it up with two details from the text.

days.ma: Quadrilaterals add up to 360°: find the missing angle with 85°, 95° and 110°. Split a regular pentagon and hexagon into triangles to find their interior angles. Classify quadrilaterals you can see at home.
days.en: Compare the two texts: what does each say about the topic, and how does the purpose change the language?

days.ma: Using a ruler and protractor, draw a triangle with a 7 cm base and angles of 40° and 65° at its ends. Measure the third angle and the other two sides. Then draw a parallelogram with sides of 6 cm and 4 cm and an angle of 60°.
days.en: Turn a chatty advert into a formal letter of complaint, using formal vocabulary, the passive and one subjunctive ('I request that the product be replaced').

days.ma: Quick check: three missing-angle questions a parent draws; name a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides; the interior angles of an octagon add up to?; one interior angle of a regular hexagon.
days.en: Quick check: a 15-minute mini paper with one fact/opinion question and one prediction question; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Consolidation: SATs-style practice (percentages, measures and statistics)

spell.rule: review: adding -ly to adjectives (frequent → frequently, definite → definitely, immediate → immediately)

weeks.read: a full SATs-style reading booklet with three texts, taken over two days

days.ma: Arithmetic practice: 15 questions in 15 minutes (long multiplication, long division, fractions, decimals, percentages, order of operations). Mark and correct together.
days.en: Reading paper day 1: read the first two texts and answer their questions in 25 minutes. Mark together and talk about any lost marks.

days.ma: Measures: area of a triangle with base 9 cm and height 8 cm; volume of a 6 × 4 × 2.5 cm cuboid; two shapes with the same area but different perimeters.
days.en: Reading paper day 2: the third text and its questions in 25 minutes. Which question types are easiest and which need more practice?

days.ma: Statistics: a pie chart shows 1/4 of 80 pupils walk to school – how many and what angle? Find the mean of 23, 31, 27 and 19.
days.en: Grammar and punctuation: 15 short questions a parent sets, including word classes, passive and active, subjunctive and semi-colons.

days.ma: Angles: missing angles on a line, at a point, opposite angles and in a triangle; the interior angle of a regular octagon.
days.en: Spelling: test yourself on this half term's words and five tricky words from earlier in the year; write a memory trick for any you miss.

days.ma: Half-term check: 3/8 as a decimal and a percentage; 40% of 65; 2 + 3 × (8 − 5); area of a parallelogram 12 cm × 4.5 cm; the mean of 8, 12, 10, 14; a missing angle in a quadrilateral. Mark and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: a two-minute talk about which reading skills you are most and least confident in, and the half-term spelling test.

weeks.title: Circles, nets and 3-D shapes + revision

spell.rule: the prefix in- becomes im- before m and p (immediate, immature, impossible, impatient)

weeks.read: a feature article or opinion column written for young readers

days.ma: Draw circles using a pencil tied to a piece of string held down at the centre. Label the centre, radius, diameter and circumference, and check the diameter is twice the radius.
days.en: Plan a persuasive article on a topic you care about (e.g. more cycle paths). Note your audience, purpose, three strong points and the evidence for each.

days.ma: Measure the diameter and circumference (using string) of five round things at home. Record them in a table: is the circumference always about three times the diameter?
days.en: Write the article, using rhetorical questions, facts, a short anecdote and a powerful final sentence.

days.ma: Unfold an empty food box to see its net. Then draw six different arrangements of six squares and test which fold into a cube.
days.en: Swap with a parent and assess each other's writing: one thing that persuades well, one fact that could be an opinion, and one sentence to improve.

days.ma: Build a triangular prism or square-based pyramid from a net drawn on card from an old box. Count its faces, edges and vertices and compare with a cube.
days.en: Edit your article in a different colour, improving vocabulary, cutting repetition and checking the register suits your reader.

days.ma: Quick check: the radius of a circle with a 15 cm diameter; which of three nets a parent draws make a cube?; faces, edges and vertices of a hexagonal prism; 3 quick arithmetic questions.
days.en: Quick check: read your article aloud and ask the family to pick out one fact and one opinion; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: SATs revision: arithmetic

spell.rule: keep the final e when adding a suffix that starts with a consonant (sincerely, definitely, achievement, hopeful)

weeks.read: a short story collection, reading one story a day for pleasure

days.en: Word classes in context: identify nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, determiners, pronouns and conjunctions in five sentences, including words that can be more than one class.

days.ma: Long multiplication and division focus: 4,152 × 37; 2,094 × 56; 7,296 ÷ 32; 9,315 ÷ 45. Estimate first, then check.
days.en: Clauses and phrases: label main clauses, subordinate clauses, relative clauses and noun phrases in six sentences. Tick the sentences that are complex.
Tenses and verb forms: name the tense in eight sentences (simple, progressive, perfect, past or present), then identify modal verbs and the subjunctive.
Punctuation: commas after fronted adverbials, apostrophes, inverted commas, colons, semi-colons, dashes and hyphens. Correct ten sentences a parent writes.

days.ma: Mini arithmetic test: 20 questions in 20 minutes covering the whole week. Mark it, record the score and pick two question types to practise again.
days.en: Quick check: a 20-question grammar and punctuation quiz a parent makes from this week's activities; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: SATs revision: reasoning with number

spell.rule: -ant and -ance go together, like -ent and -ence (relevant → relevance, observant → observance, tolerant → tolerance)

weeks.read: an adventure story extract and a related information text

days.ma: Two-step problems: a school buys 14 boxes of 36 pencils and gives out 287. How many are left? Show your method and an estimate check.
days.en: Prefixes and suffixes: build as many words as you can from 'act', 'form' and 'port' in five minutes, then explain how each prefix or suffix changes the meaning.

days.ma: Negative numbers and place value reasoning: the temperature was −7 °C and rose 12 degrees, then fell 9 degrees. Which digit changes when you add 300,000 to 6,850,421?
days.en: Silent letters and tricky words: a parent reads 15 words with silent letters and from this year's lists; write them, then check and correct.

days.ma: Ratio and algebra: the ratio of red to blue counters is 2:7 and there are 45 counters – how many are red? Find pairs that satisfy 4a + b = 25.
days.en: Homophones and near-homophones: write sentences for aloud/allowed, cereal/serial, guessed/guest, precede/proceed, affect/effect.

days.ma: Rounding and reasoning: a car travels 37.8 km each way to work, five days a week. How far in a week, to the nearest 10 km? Which answer makes sense in context?
days.en: Read an adventure extract and answer retrieval, inference and word-meaning questions in 15 minutes. Use roots to explain one unfamiliar word.

days.ma: Quick check: a mixed set of six reasoning questions a parent chooses from this week's types. Explain your thinking aloud for one of them.
days.en: Quick check: 20 spelling words from the year with a parent, and correct any errors with a dictionary.

weeks.title: SATs revision: reasoning with measures, shape and statistics

spell.rule: -ary and -ery endings where the vowel is hard to hear (secretary, cemetery, library, stationery)

weeks.read: SATs-style practice texts, timed

days.ma: Measures: 2.5 kg of flour makes 20 loaves – how many grams per loaf? 48 km in miles; 3 hours 45 minutes in minutes; a cuboid's volume with sides 8 cm, 5 cm and 4.5 cm.
days.en: Timed reading: one text and its questions in 20 minutes. Practise moving on when stuck and coming back at the end.

days.ma: Shape: missing angles in a triangle and on a line; the area of a triangle with base 15 cm and height 8 cm; the area of a parallelogram with base 12 cm and height 7 cm.
days.en: Author's language: choose three phrases from a description and explain the effect of each on the reader in a full sentence.

days.ma: Position and direction: plot a shape in all four quadrants, translate it 3 left and 5 down, then reflect the original in the x-axis. Write all the coordinates.
days.en: Non-fiction: retrieve and record information from a text into a table, then write one sentence comparing two facts.

days.ma: Statistics: draw a line graph from a table a parent gives; interpret a pie chart of 40 pupils' favourite sports; find a missing value when the mean of five numbers is 12.
days.en: Mixed question types: fact and opinion, true and false, sequencing and a three-mark explanation, all from one text.

days.ma: Quick check: six reasoning questions across measures, geometry and statistics. Mark them, then explain one answer as if you were the teacher.
days.en: Quick check: a 20-minute reading paper section; talk about which strategies helped; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: SATs week: calm, short warm-ups

spell.rule: -ain at the end of a word sounds like 'in' (bargain, captain, mountain, certain)

weeks.read: something just for pleasure: comics, joke books or a favourite reread

days.ma: Gentle warm-up: five mental questions over breakfast (e.g. 25% of 80, 7 × 0.6, 1,000 − 365). Then play a family game of target number with digit cards.
days.en: Read anything you like for 20 minutes – a favourite reread is perfect – and tell someone the best bit.

days.ma: Fraction, decimal and percentage snap with your matching cards from earlier in the year, then stop – no extra practice needed tonight.
days.en: Read a funny poem aloud to the family, using voices and timing to get laughs.

days.ma: Order of operations dice game: roll three dice (or draw three digit cards) and use +, −, ×, ÷ and brackets to make as many target numbers from 1 to 20 as you can.
days.en: Family book chat: each person describes a book they loved at your age, and you recommend one to them.

days.ma: Times-table and division facts quiz for 10 minutes, then a relaxed walk counting in decimals and fractions (0.25, 0.5, 0.75…).
days.en: Perform a short piece you have written this year – a poem, speech or story opening – to someone new, like a grandparent on a call.

days.ma: Celebration check: tell a parent which maths you felt most confident about this week and one thing you are proud of. No test today.
days.en: Celebration: choose a new book for after the tests and write a short note to yourself about how the week went.

weeks.title: Consolidation: after the tests

spell.rule: review: the letters ui making 'oo' or 'i' sounds (nuisance, bruise, fruit, suit, guide, build)

weeks.read: a gripping adventure novel to start now the tests are over

days.ma: Place value and factor puzzle: make the largest seven-digit multiple of 5 from digit cards, then find a number between 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 with exactly three different prime factors.
days.en: Plan an adventure story of your own with a twist ending, thinking about how authors in your reading build tension.

days.ma: Design a garden on squared paper with an area of 48 m² but the longest possible perimeter. Then design one with the same area and shortest perimeter.
days.en: Write the opening of your adventure: a vivid setting, a character with a clear want, and dialogue that moves the action on.

days.ma: Make an open box from a net of card: what size squares should you cut from the corners of a 20 cm square sheet to hold the most cubes? Try three sizes.
days.en: Write the middle and the twist, using a range of sentence types, cohesive links between paragraphs and at least two punctuation marks you have learnt this year.

days.ma: Draw a sequence of growing patterns and describe the rule; scale a drawing of your house by scale factor 1/2; count how many different sandwiches can be made from 4 fillings and 3 breads.
days.en: Proof-read and edit, then write a final copy in your best joined handwriting at a steady speed.

days.ma: Half-term check: a mixed set of ten questions from the whole year, marked together. Choose one topic to practise over the half-term break in short bursts.
days.en: Quick check: read your adventure aloud to the family and ask for one star and one wish; take the half-term spelling test.

weeks.title: Project: design a dream bedroom

spell.rule: -our endings in British English (neighbour, behaviour, honour, rumour, colour)

weeks.read: an autobiography or memoir written for young readers

days.ma: Measure your bedroom and draw an accurate scale plan on squared paper, choosing a sensible scale (such as 1 cm to 25 cm).
days.en: Read a memoir extract and notice how the writer chooses only the memories that matter. List five moments from your own primary school years you could write about.

days.ma: Design new furniture for your plan: cut scale shapes from paper for a bed, desk and wardrobe and arrange them so there is space to walk.
days.en: Plan your own autobiography chapter: 'My Primary Years'. Choose an audience (your future self or a younger child) and arrange your memories into paragraphs.

days.ma: Calculate the floor area and the area of each wall, minus a door and window. How much paint is needed if 1 litre covers 12 m²?
days.en: Write the first half, using vivid detail, a flashback and a thesaurus to find precise words for your feelings.

days.ma: Set a pretend budget of £400. Price items from a catalogue or website, apply a 15% discount on one item and check you stay within budget.
days.en: Write the second half, ending with a reflection on how you have changed since your first day in Reception.

days.ma: Final check: present your design to the family with the plan, areas, costs and one reason for each choice. Answer their questions.
days.en: Quick check: read your favourite paragraph aloud and say why you chose it; spell this week's word and three other -our words.

weeks.title: Project: family survey and statistics report

spell.rule: words with an unstressed middle syllable that is easy to miss when speaking (vegetable, temperature, chocolate, interest)

weeks.read: information about secondary school life: school websites, prospectuses and guides for new pupils

days.ma: Design a survey question for at least 20 people (family, neighbours, friends by message), such as 'What is your favourite vegetable?' Make a tally chart for the answers.
days.en: Research your secondary school (or secondary schools in general): find and record five facts about the timetable, subjects and clubs from its website or prospectus.

days.ma: Turn your results into fractions and percentages of the total. Round each percentage to the nearest whole number and check they add up to about 100%.
days.en: Note-taking: list ten new words you may meet at secondary (timetable, homework planner, laboratory). Check each in a dictionary and write a definition.

days.ma: Draw a pie chart of your results, working out each angle from the fraction of 360°. Then collect a second set of data with numbers (e.g. how many minutes people spend reading a day) and find the mean.
days.en: Write a short guide for a Year 6 pupil about starting secondary, with headings, bullet points and a tips box.

days.ma: Draw a line graph of something that changes over a day or week (the temperature at noon, or how many steps you walk) and write three sentences interpreting it.
days.en: Turn your guide into a three-minute presentation with notes on cards, and rehearse it.

days.ma: Final check: present your survey report with the pie chart, the mean and the line graph, and answer three questions from the family.
days.en: Quick check: give your presentation, then answer questions using your notes; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Ready for secondary: timetables, journeys and money

spell.rule: single and double letters in tricky words: harass has one r and two s; embarrass has two of each

weeks.read: a short playscript, or a story written as a play

days.ma: Plan the journey to your secondary school: the distance in km and miles, the time it takes walking and by bus, and the time you need to leave to arrive by 08:40.
days.en: Read a short playscript. Notice stage directions, character names, the lack of speech marks and how the dialogue tells the story.

days.ma: Read a real bus or train timetable (printed or online). Answer: which service gets you there before 08:30? How long is the journey? What if it is 15 minutes late?
days.en: Plan a scene about the first day at a new school with three characters, a problem and a funny or touching resolution.

days.ma: Make a weekly secondary timetable on paper with five lessons a day. Work out the total minutes of maths and English in a week and convert to hours and minutes.
days.en: Write the playscript scene, using stage directions in the present tense and dialogue that shows each character's personality.

days.ma: Lunch money: with £12.50 a week, plan five lunches from a pretend menu with prices; how much is left? If prices rise by 8%, what changes? Round sensibly.
days.en: Rehearse the scene with family members, thinking about volume, movement and timing.

days.ma: Final check: a journey problem from a parent that includes timetables, distance in miles and km, and money. Explain each step.
days.en: Quick check: perform your scene, then explain one choice the playwright made in the script you read; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: Puzzles and investigations: a taste of secondary maths

spell.rule: ou making a long 'oh' sound (shoulder, mould, boulder, soul)

weeks.read: speeches and debates written for young people

days.ma: Number line challenge: −5 + 8, 3 − 9, −4 − 6 and −2 × 3. Use a long number line and talk about what happens when you subtract to below zero.
days.en: Choose a debate motion such as 'Homework should be banned at secondary school'. List arguments for and against, and mark which are facts and which are opinions.

days.ma: Prime investigation: is every even number from 4 to 40 the sum of two primes? Record a pair for each and look for a pattern.
days.en: Write a one-minute opening speech for your side using formal register, a rhetorical question and the subjunctive ('I propose that every pupil be given…').

days.ma: Handshake puzzle: if everyone at a party of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 people shakes hands once, how many handshakes? Find the pattern and predict for 10 people.
days.en: Prepare rebuttals: write three responses that politely challenge the other side ('Although some argue…, the evidence suggests…').

days.ma: Two unknowns: tickets cost £3 for children and £5 for adults, and a group paid £34. Find all the possible groups. Then write a formula for the cost of c children and a adults.
days.en: Hold the family debate with a chairperson, timings and a vote at the end.

days.ma: Final check: invent a puzzle of your own using a sequence or a formula, solve it, and test it on the family.
days.en: Quick check: explain why you voted the way you did, giving reasons and evidence; spell this week's word.

weeks.title: End-of-primary project: memory book, part 1 + number review

spell.rule: number words: four and fourteen keep the u, but forty does not (forty, ninth, twelfth)

weeks.read: a story about endings and new beginnings, and favourite books from across primary school

days.ma: Memory book maths page: how many days, hours and minutes have you spent at primary school? (Assume 190 school days a year and 6.5 hours a day.) Write the answers in words and round them sensibly.
days.en: Start a memory book: plan the pages (my best memories, my favourite books, people who helped me, advice for younger pupils, my hopes for secondary).

days.ma: How many books have you read at primary? Estimate a total, then use long multiplication to work out how many pages that might be if the average book has 168 pages.
days.en: Write 'My favourite books' page: three books you loved at primary and what each taught you, quoting a line or describing a moment.

days.ma: Plan a leavers' picnic for 12 people: share costs fairly, find the fraction each person pays, and work out what fraction of the food is sandwiches, fruit and cake.
days.en: Read a story about an ending or a new beginning. Explain how the author makes the reader feel at the end, using two quotations.

days.ma: Order of operations puzzle page for younger pupils: write five calculations with brackets and their answers, plus one with a mistake for them to find.
days.en: Write 'Advice for younger pupils': five tips with reasons, using root words or prefixes you learnt this year to explain any long words.

days.ma: Final check: ten questions on place value, rounding, long multiplication, long division, fractions and percentages. Mark and talk about the trickiest.
days.en: Quick check: share two memory book pages with the family and spell this week's word.

weeks.title: End-of-primary project: memory book, part 2 + measures, shape and statistics review

spell.rule: review: double letters from Latin prefixes (according, accompany, attached, suggest, aggressive)

weeks.read: the memory book itself, and the year's favourite poems

days.ma: Class statistics page: ask friends or family for their heights in cm, find the mean, and draw a pie chart of favourite subjects from at least 12 people.
days.en: Grammar showcase page: write a short paragraph about your time at primary that includes a passive sentence, a subjunctive, a relative clause and a modal verb, then label them.

days.ma: Build a memory box from a net drawn on card, with dimensions you choose. Calculate its volume in cm³ and check if your keepsakes will fit.
days.en: Punctuation challenge: write about your favourite school trip using a semi-colon, a colon, a dash, brackets and a hyphenated adjective.

days.ma: Draw a map of your primary school on a four-quadrant grid, giving the coordinates of key places (hall, office, playground).
days.en: Spelling and word page: list ten words you have learnt to spell this year with their tricky parts highlighted, and five homophones you now get right.

days.ma: Measures quiz for the memory book: your height in m and mm, your mass in kg and g, and the distance from home to school in km and miles.
days.en: Edit and proof-read all of your memory book pages, improving vocabulary and making sure the tense is consistent.

days.ma: Final check: measure, convert and calculate – an angle question, an area question, a volume question and a mean question. Mark together.
days.en: Quick check: use grammar terms to explain three sentences in your memory book, and spell ten words from the year.

weeks.title: End-of-primary celebration: finish and present the memory book

spell.rule: spell-it-right: words for your memory book and your letter to your future self

weeks.read: the child's free choice, plus a list of books to try over the summer

days.ma: Plan a family celebration tea: a budget of £30, prices with a 10% discount on one item, and quantities for the number of guests.
days.en: Write a letter to your future self to open at the end of Year 7: what you hope for, what you are proud of and one piece of advice.

days.ma: Make a timetable for the celebration in 24-hour time, with how long each part lasts and the total time.
days.en: Write the final memory book page in your neatest joined handwriting, choosing the best pen for headings and captions.

days.ma: Design a celebration game with a formula for scoring (e.g. points = 3 × hits + 2), then play and record the scores.
days.en: Write and rehearse a short speech to thank the people who helped you through primary school.

days.ma: Hold the celebration (or part of it): measure, record and compare results from the game in a table; work out each player's percentage of the total score.
days.en: Make a list of summer books to try, with a sentence for each explaining why you chose it.

days.ma: Final check: answer the family's questions on the year's maths and explain one topic you are proud to have mastered.
days.en: Celebration: present your memory book, deliver your speech and share your summer reading list.
